finding.claim: POST /profile/avatar fetches an attacker-supplied URL with axios, which follows redirects by default. The only check is startsWith('https://') on the initial URL, so an attacker can redirect to internal or metadata addresses (including HTTPS-to-HTTP redirects).

trace.note: avatarUrl read directly from JSON body
only typeof string and startsWith('https://') checked; host not parsed or validated
axios GET with default redirect following (maxRedirects not set to 0); no per-hop check, no IP block, no timeout
response length returned to client as bytes, a size oracle on internal responses

finding.guards_checked: Only the https:// prefix check on the initial string. No host parsing, private/loopback/link-local/metadata blocking, redirect limit or re-validation, IP pinning, timeout, or size limit. No package.json or lockfile present, so axios version could not be verified; default redirect following is standard across versions.

verdict.guard_found: none. The only check is typeof and startsWith("https://") at server.js:11, which is a prefix check and does not close the finding. No host parsing, IP/private-range blocking, maxRedirects: 0, or timeout appears at server.js:14. The POST /profile/avatar route has no auth middleware (server.js:9), so the source is reachable by an unauthenticated caller.
verdict.reason: req.body.avatarUrl (server.js:10) is attacker-controlled and only prefix-checked (server.js:11) before axios.get(url) (server.js:14), which follows redirects by default; the response size is returned to the caller (server.js:15). Every trace line matches the file. The axios version could not be verified (no package.json or lockfile), but default redirect following is standard. Even without the redirect, the https:// prefix alone lets the attacker name an internal https host directly, so the SSRF holds regardless of the redirect detail.

finding.claim: GET /users/:id encodes the id with encodeURIComponent, so the host is fixed and slashes are encoded. If the upstream user service decodes %2F before routing, a double-encoded id such as ..%2F..%2Fadmin reaches other internal paths. Medium-low confidence: depends on upstream behavior not visible in this repo.

trace.note: route param :id, decoded once by Express, so ../../admin arrives as the value
encodeURIComponent re-encodes slashes to %2F; host and query/fragment injection blocked
URL built with encoded id; upstream decoding %2F would yield path traversal on users.internal

finding.guards_checked: encodeURIComponent blocks host change and ?/# injection. No id format validation. Upstream routing behavior not verifiable from this repo.

verdict.guard_found: server.js:19 encodeURIComponent(req.params.id) encodes "/", "?", and "#", but it is not one of the closing guard types (no hostname membership or anchored match), and there is no id format validation; the host is a fixed constant at server.js:7.
verdict.reason: The trace lines at server.js:18-20 are accurate and the id is attacker-controlled via the path, but the claimed path traversal only occurs if users.internal decodes %2F before routing (not visible in this repo), so the impact cannot be decided from this code; the claim's "double-encoded" example is also wrong, since the working payload is single-encoded (..%2F..%2Fadmin), which Express decodes to ../../admin at server.js:18 and encodeURIComponent re-encodes at server.js:19.
